"It is one of the most ancient surviving commoners' rights in England, thought to date at least to the Norman conquest if not before.

But the custom of allowing sheep to roam freely in the Forest of Dean in Gloucestershire is set to be criminalised in one village, in the latest manifestation of controversial new antisocial behaviour laws nicknamed the “busybodies’ charter”.

Under plans drawn up by Forest of Dean District Council, anyone allowing sheep to “enter and remain” in Bream, the area’s largest village, will be committing a crime, facing a fine of up to £1,000.

Introduced almost two years ago, so-called Public Spaces Protection Orders (PSPOs) allow councils to ban specific activities within certain areas to crack down on threatening or violent behaviour.

The Manifesto Club think-tank has catalogued how the orders have already been used to outlaw lucky charms, chalk drawings, singing and even, in one case, carrying a golf bag.

Touts offering punting trips or ghost tours in Cambridge have also been hit with the restrictions.

But it is the first time they are known to have been used to criminalise sheep.

It follows complaints of sheep nibbling rose bushes, baaing loudly and leaving droppings on pavements without cleaning up after them.

The council set up a special “Irresponsible Shepherding Scrutiny Task Group” to compile what it describes as “evidence logs” cataloguing the “sheep nuisance”.

Its subsequent report bemoans “misery to residents” caused by the woolly visitors.

Shepherds believe at least some of the complaints come from new arrivals to the area as part of “gentrification”, many of whom ignore the unwritten rule of fencing and gating gardens off in favour of installing large open driveways.

They fear it could spell the end of rights enjoyed for centuries which allow commoners in the “Hundred of St Briavels” – the traditional name for the Forest of Dean – to “turn out” or graze sheep freely. They are planning a protest outside the council buildings on Saturday, accompanied by dogs and sheep.

The custom is credited with shaping the area’s landscape and ecosystems including helping create one of Britain’s biggest colonies of horseshoe bats, which feed on dung beetle.

Shepherds - known as "sheep badgers" - say local herds are only now beginning to reach levels seen before the foot and mouth crisis in 2001.

Mick Holder, secretary of the area’s Commoners Association, voiced fears that other villages could follow suit if the order in Bream, currently under consultation, is enforced.

“When the free roaming is finished that’s when the forest starts to die,” he said.

“We saw a situation in 2001 when there were no sheep out and about for 12 months.

“During that period lots of people commented 'what has happened to our road, we can’t walk through the woods any more, the undergrowth has become the overgrowth'.”

He added: “A lot of the complaints we were getting were just somebody saying ‘there were sheep walking down the street last night mind’ or ‘there were sheep bleating outside my house’.”

He emphasised that not all of the complaints had come from incomers but that basic measures which would solve many problems were not being taken.

“The rule of thumb in the Forest here is that you must fence against the forest,” he explained.

“That applies to forester and foreigner alike.

“Now a lot of people have chosen to ignore that.

“They have maybe got two or three cars so they want to take the wall down and the gate down.

“That is not acceptable practice.”

Josie Appleton, convenor of the Manifesto Club, said: “This criminalising of sheep is taking PSPOs beyond the draconian into the realms of farce.

“Increasingly, every minor inconvenience of everyday life is leading to a new criminal law.

“Discussion and negotiation would be far better approaches than putting shepherds in the dock.”

The statement from Forest of Dean District Council said: "The Council supports the tradition of free roaming sheep within the district and accepts that the vast majority of sheep owners are responsible.

"However, complaints have been received regarding the irresponsible shepherding of sheep, particularly in the village of Bream. These complaints led to the Council undertaking a full scrutiny inquiry."
